posts.cooked:
Hello world. I picked up Sentinels of the Multiverse yesterday and have, since, played four games. Two by myself. One that was apparently bad and unrecommended. I would point out at this point that I've thoroughly enjoyed the game, but really, who would buy a game, play it four times including twice on their own in two days, and then specifically hunt out that game's forum to say that they didn't like it? ...Well, jerks would.

I actually picked up Sentinel Tactics first, a few weeks ago - and still haven't played it yet, because a great deal of my skirmish gaming time has been going to Imperial Assault recently. (I've got a campaign going with my sister, it's close to the end, but she gets to play Empire next time.) Right beside it was a set of plastic-packed dirt cheap promo expansions, so I thought "how could I lose?" and grabbed a couple. Turns out they were for base Sentinels, not Tactics. And thus, I ended up with Miss Information and the Final Wasteland before anything else.

(...Which isn't really a good combination, thematically. "Mr. Parsons, I know you're currently in a horrifying wasteland surrounded by New Jersey Devils, tikbalangs, and Slenderman, but you really need to go get a 'cat' out of a 'tree'. Mu ha ha ha ha ha ha.")

While I had no idea what I was looking at, and frankly looking at Miss Information's cards to get an idea of what the game is like is a losing bet to start with because her mechanics are strange and unusual, I was intrigued enough to pick up the game a few weeks later, and still haven't fought Aminia to date. Well, like I said, she's tricky. I started at my weekly game night where five of us, playing Haka, Tachyon, Fanatic, Bunker, and the Wraith took down Baron Blade in the Wagner Mars Base with unusual ease. I suspect that the Wraith getting her Micro-Targeting Computer and Razor Ordnance on the first two turns was a strong influence, while Haka doing what Haka does cleaned up pretty much anything other than Baron Blade in short order, and Fanatic pulled out Absolution on her first turn, wailed on the Baron with it for a while while burning down her own HP with Embolden, and then pulled out an 18 point Wrathful Retribution to finish him off. So he didn't get to do much or, to be honest, present much of a threat after his first two Slash and Burns - it was really Mars doing most of the damage. But I honestly like Baron Blade, so I do hope he gets his chance to pummel a team I'm playing to the skin of our teeth before long.

Other games were my sister (Fanatic: she's a big fan of 'rend, slaughter, devour your enemies!' recently) and myself (Tempest and Tachyon) against Baron Blade in Megalopolis, where he managed to get nine cards in his trash before flipping, but then got worn down by withering police fire; myself in a Sidekick-randomised game where the app decided to give me Tachyon and Tempest again, but to add Legacy to the play, against Citizen Dawn on Insula Primalis, where she proved tenacious by starting out with Citizens Hammer and Anvil and getting Return With The Dawn on her first play; and myself with the Visionary and Ra against Omnitron in the Final Wasteland, where I learned why two heroes are not really enough heroes.

I said that I honestly like Baron Blade, but really that's not unusual, because I honestly like all of the characters. I'm proving quite taken with Dawn's harsh cult-of-personality zealotry, and while I originally thought that Aminia was going to be a fairly typical femme fatale, I then read her incredibly tragic backstory and may have "aww!"d aloud. I had expected that Haka would end up being my favourite hero character - I've a friend who's big on Hawaii and Hawaiian culture, and described Haka to him as "a Polynesian Hulk", which drew his attention - but Tachyon ended up stealing my affection. Faster than I could notice, natch. While her cards and mechanics work beautifully - a good Lightspeed Barrage in the late game is a wonderful finisher - I'm also tremendously fond of her always-on-the-go cheerful Dr. Horrible quoting personality. (I'm still curious as to who the "dude" on Fleet of Foot who is most definitely "not (her) nemesis" is.)

...Anyway, I'm sure none of this was new, interesting, or enlightening in any way, but since I always like babbling and listening to babbling about games I like, here is some babbling about a game I like, and since I'm sure almost everyone who visits this forum also likes that game, maybe you'll like 'listening' to said babble. Thank you and goodnight.

posts.name: VisforYoshi
posts.cooked: Welcome tot the forums (I'm sure you'll be getting that a lot). Like Powerhound said, getting the digital version is a good idea, because not only does it keep track of everything and make single player games easier, but it may also teach you some mechanincs that you missed the first time. I realized I've been misplaying not just omnitron, but also some of Dawn's cards after looking at the digital version, so it's a good way to show you how to play in the physical version properly. It also helps teach you some of the more complex heros you'll see in the game (I'm looking at you, Argent Adept fans). If you ever get tired of just the base set, I would reccomend the rook city/infernal relic double pack to start, because not only does it come with two bonus expansions, but also another box for storing all the cards. Shattered timelines is also a good choice because the villains are varying difficulties, and the heros are pretty solid (A lot of people I know started with chrono-ranger). This is also a good place to get tips on heros, villians and the like, because the people here are awesome

posts.name: Sailboat
posts.cooked:
Welcome! I too recommend expansions, not only because they give you cool new heroes and villains to play with, but also because having a wider variety of characters keeps the original characters fresh longer. After finding many things to love in the expansions, I find myself discovering new appreciation for many of the older heroes and villains.

One of the subtleties about Sentinels I enjoy is how each character not only has distinct flavor text, but also their decks play differently in ways that reflect the character’s powers and personality. Using combinations of simple mechanics like draw and discard, the designers have given the characters unique feel.

The example most frequently cited is your beloved Tachyon. The flurry of cards she burns through just feels fast – and the way she builds inexorably toward a big finish feels like you’re accelerating toward a gigantic collision. All achieved through fairly simple deck mechanics.

Legacy’s card choices really feel like you’re both looking out for your friends and encouraging them, with a healthy dose of self-sacrifice thrown in. Speaking of self-sacrifice, one poster memorably called Fanatic’s deck “dramatic.” She’s always willing to take damage not to protect her friends so much as to mete out justice with a flaming sword!

Haka is supposed to enjoy battle. You can see that in his card illustrations, but you can also feel it in his strong card draw and self-healing, coupled with his steady regular damage-dealing and huge surge capacity. He doesn’t control much, but his deck was born to fight it out, and you’ll be able to do so more confidently with his mechanics.

In later expansions you’ll run into Nightmist, who deals with dark powers at fearful cost to her personal safety in order to keep our realm safe. Her gameplay wonderfully encapsulates this theme. And Parse, an Asberger’s-Syndrome-afflicted heroine whose mind was merged with Omnitron’s vast computing power. Her gameplay is extremely analytical and precise.

And on and on. Even the villains – the inexorable advance of the moon as Baron Blade torments the heroes is accomplished through the simplest of card mechanics, but the pressure is real. There’s a gret deal of artful subtlety in Sentinels of the Multiverse. I hope you enjoy it for a long time to come!
